searchNote: WebSearch worked; WebFetch could not resolve hosts. The per-turn web search budget (shared by all agents) ran out partway through, so about half of the planned searches were not run. Claims not searched were kept only where I am certain from solid knowledge or where they agree with the library's own work records (checked locally with grep); the rest are listed under remainingDoubts. The library's work records were themselves only spot-checked, so agreement with them is corroboration, not proof.

corrected.was: Art Spiegelman's Maus (book form 1986; a special Pulitzer Prize citation in 1992)
corrected.now: Art Spiegelman's Maus (first book volume 1986; a special Pulitzer Prize citation in 1992)
corrected.why: 1986 is the first volume only; the second volume came in 1991, so 'book form 1986' implied the whole work.

softened.was: Famous Funnies (1934) is widely called the first American comic book
softened.now: Famous Funnies (1934) is often called the first true American comic book, though promotional giveaways of reprinted strips came earlier
softened.why: Historians' phrase is 'first true' comic book; Eastern Color's 1933 Funnies on Parade giveaway of reprinted strips preceded it, so a bare 'first' overstates.

softened.was: Mort Walker's Lexicon of Comicana (1980) popularised both words.
softened.now: Mort Walker's Lexicon of Comicana (1980) helped popularise both words.
softened.why: Walker's 1964 article introduced 'grawlix' before the book, and he later credited the idea to Charles D. Rice; no source found for who coined 'emanata'. 'Helped popularise' claims no coinage.

softened.was: Scott McCloud's Understanding Comics (1993) is the standard study of how comics work
softened.now: Scott McCloud's Understanding Comics (1993) is a widely read study of how comics work
softened.why: 'The standard study' is a judgement stated as fact.

softened.was: Chris Ware's Jimmy Corrigan, the Smartest Kid on Earth (2000) shows how far layout can carry feeling.
softened.now: Chris Ware's Jimmy Corrigan, the Smartest Kid on Earth (2000) is often praised for how far its layout carries feeling.
softened.why: An evaluative claim about a work, now attributed to critical opinion.

remainingDoubts: Hogarth as an ancestor of comics and Toepffer as 'a father of the modern comic' are historians' conventions; the text hedges both.
Famous Funnies: sources disagree on which 1934 issue was first sold on newsstands (February, May and July are all given). The text avoids dating it beyond 1934.
Kyle: sources differ on the essay title and issue. The text says only 'a 1964 fan essay'.

Grawlix and emanata: a coiner is not established for emanata, and Walker credited Rice for grawlix in 1975. The text now claims only 'helped popularise'; the tropes record says Walker 'catalogued and jokingly named' marks, which does not claim coinage.
Maus Pulitzer: some sources say the special citation was for the second volume only. The text says only 'a special Pulitzer Prize citation in 1992'.

Not searched, from solid knowledge: Watchmen as 'largely nine-panel pages', McCloud's simple-face argument, 'about 20 to 22 story pages' for a monthly (hedged with 'roughly' and 'practice differs'), the Marvel method description, 1930s Hergé start in Belgium.

corrected.was: Boys' love (BL) and yuri: romance genres about male couples, largely written by and for women, and about women; both have their own magazines and sections in shops.
corrected.now: Boys' love (BL) and yuri: BL is romance about male couples, largely written by and for women, and yuri is romance about women; both have their own magazines and sections in shops.
corrected.why: The original could be read as saying BL is about women. Meaning is now unambiguous; no new claim added.

remainingDoubts: Year 24 Group: membership is loosely defined. The text names Hagio and Takemiya as the group and Ikeda as a 'contemporary', which is the safest wording; the library's shojo entry lists Ikeda as a member.
Shonen Jump's 1968 launch date varies by source (July or August cover dates). The text gives only the year, and the 1969 switch to weekly is supported.

Not searched and not checkable against the library: 'weekly shonen chapters often around twenty pages' (hedged), 'weekly magazines widely reported to use reader surveys', print magazine sales falling since the 1990s (no figures given), English editions 'usually' keeping right-to-left reading, teen and older teen age ratings, example titles by audience category, and Comiket's 1975 start.
BL being 'largely written by and for women' is a common generalisation and is hedged with 'largely'.

corrected.was: Some creators shared comics on early online services in the 1980s and 1990s, before the web;
corrected.now: Some creators shared comics on early online services in the 1980s and early 1990s, before the web;
corrected.why: The web spread from the early 1990s, and conv 2 starts there, so 'and 1990s, before the web' was inconsistent.

corrected.was: the vertical-scroll webtoon, begun on Korea's Naver Webtoon in 2004, spread worldwide
corrected.now: the vertical-scroll webtoon, which grew out of South Korean web portals (Daum from 2003, Naver Webtoon from 2004), spread worldwide
corrected.why: Daum launched a commercial webtoon service in 2003, before Naver, and no source isolates Naver as the origin of vertical scrolling.

corrected.was: as when browsers stopped supporting Flash after Adobe ended its support at the end of 2020.
corrected.now: as when Adobe ended its support for Flash at the end of 2020 and browsers followed by dropping it.
corrected.why: Order of events: Adobe's end-of-support date was 31 December 2020 and browsers removed Flash after it; the original blurred this.

corrected.was: it is also called title text or alt text.
corrected.now: it is also called title text, or loosely alt text.
corrected.why: The hover caption is the HTML title attribute; calling it alt text is common usage but technically loose.

softened.was: and many webcomic creators were prominent early users.
softened.now: and many webcomic creators have used both.
softened.why: 'Prominent early users' could not be verified; 'have used both' is safe and true.

remainingDoubts: Heartstopper's print year is deliberately left out because sources differ between 2018 and 2019.
The vertical-scroll format's exact origin is not settled in the sources I found; the text says only that it grew out of South Korean portals.
Keenspot's launch month differs by source (February or March 2000); the text gives only the year.
Not searched: Penny Arcade 1998, Questionable Content 2003, Order of the Stick 2003, xkcd 2005, Kickstarter 2009 and Patreon 2013 dates (all from solid knowledge).

Market statements (free to read, paid early access on some platforms, burnout as a common reason webcomics stop, 'story shapes often seen' in webtoons) are general practice as of 2025 with no figures, and are hedged as observations.
